name: Apple Scab
description: A common fungal disease of apple caused by Venturia inaequalis. It affects leaves and fruit and is favored by cool, wet spring weather.
symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown or black velvety spots on leaves
Distorted, curled, or puckered leaves
Premature leaf drop
Corky, scabby lesions on fruit surface
causes: Fungal infection by Venturia inaequalis
Spores overwintering in fallen, infected leaves
Cool, wet conditions during spring bud break
prevention: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves each autumn
Prune trees to improve air circulation and sunlight penetration
Choose scab-resistant apple varieties where possible
Avoid overhead irrigation that keeps foliage wet
management: Apply protectant fungicides timed to bud break and wet periods, following label and local extension guidance
Remove and dispose of infected leaves and fruit

name: Black Rot
description: A fungal disease of apple caused by Botryosphaeria obtusa, affecting leaves, fruit, and wood.
symptoms: Purple-bordered circular leaf spots ("frogeye leaf spot")
Brown to black rotted areas on fruit with concentric rings
Sunken cankers on branches and limbs
Fruit may shrivel into hard "mummies"
causes: Fungal infection by Botryosphaeria obtusa
Entry through wounds, dead wood, or old cankers
Warm, humid weather favoring fungal spread
prevention: Prune out dead, diseased, or cankered wood
Remove mummified fruit from the tree and ground
Maintain overall tree vigor and good sanitation
management: Apply fungicide programs where warranted, per local extension guidance
Promptly remove and destroy infected plant material

name: Cedar Apple Rust
description: A fungal disease caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae that requires both apple and juniper/cedar trees to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface
Orange, gelatinous spore-producing structures on leaf undersides
Distorted or spotted fruit
causes: Fungal spores alternating between apple and nearby juniper/cedar hosts
Wet spring weather favoring spore release and infection
prevention: Remove nearby juniper/cedar hosts where feasible and practical
Choose rust-resistant apple varieties
Maintain distance between apple trees and juniper/cedar hosts
management: Apply protectant fungicides during the spring infection period where warranted

description: A fungal disease of cherry caused by Podosphaera clandestina, affecting leaves and shoots.
symptoms: White, powdery fungal growth on leaves and shoots
Leaf curling and distortion
Stunted shoot growth
causes: Fungal infection favored by warm days and cool nights with moderate humidity
Airborne spore spread
prevention: Prune for good air circulation
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
Choose resistant varieties where available
management: Apply fungicide when conditions favor disease development
Remove heavily infected shoots

name: Gray Leaf Spot
description: A fungal disease of corn caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis (also called Cercospora leaf spot), producing lesions bound by leaf veins.
symptoms: Small tan to brown rectangular lesions bound by leaf veins
Lesions may merge and turn gray as they mature
Premature death of lower leaves in severe cases
causes: Fungal infection favored by warm, humid weather
Survival of the fungus in corn residue left on the soil surface
Continuous corn planting in the same field
prevention: Rotate crops away from corn
Manage or till under corn residue
Choose resistant hybrids where available
management: Apply fungicide in high-risk fields per local extension guidance

name: Common Rust
description: A fungal disease of corn caused by Puccinia sorghi.
symptoms: Small, circular to elongate cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules may darken as the season progresses
causes: Windborne fungal spores
Cool, moist conditions favoring infection
prevention: Choose resistant hybrids where available
management: Apply fungicide if infection is severe and occurs early in the season

name: Northern Leaf Blight
description: A fungal disease of corn caused by Exserohilum turcicum.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, gray-green to tan lesions on leaves
Lesions may merge, leading to significant leaf area loss
causes: Fungal spores surviving in corn residue
Moderate temperatures and high humidity favoring spread
prevention: Choose resistant hybrids where available
Rotate crops
Manage crop residue
management: Apply fungicide where warranted per local extension guidance

name: Black Rot
description: A fungal disease of grape caused by Guignardia bidwellii, affecting leaves and fruit.
symptoms: Small brown circular leaf spots with dark margins
Berries shrivel into hard black "mummies"
Lesions may also appear on shoots and tendrils
causes: Fungal spores overwintering in mummified fruit and infected canes
Warm, wet weather favoring spread
prevention: Remove mummified fruit and infected canes during dormant pruning
Improve canopy airflow through proper training and pruning
management: Apply fungicide programs timed with grape growth stages per local extension guidance

name: Esca (Black Measles)
description: A complex trunk disease of grapevine associated with several wood-colonizing fungi, affecting the vine's vascular system.
symptoms: Interveinal "tiger-stripe" discoloration on leaves
Small dark spots on berries
Internal wood decay
Sudden vine collapse in severe cases
causes: Fungal colonization of trunk and wood, often entering through pruning wounds
Chronic, cumulative trunk disease that develops over years
prevention: Use careful pruning practices and avoid wounding during wet periods
Protect pruning cuts
Avoid pruning during periods of active fungal spore release
management: No reliable cure once established; remove and destroy severely affected wood or vines
Trunk renewal may be attempted in some cases per local viticultural extension guidance

name: Leaf Blight (Isariopsis Leaf Spot)
description: A fungal leaf disease of grape caused by Pseudocercospora vitis (also known as Isariopsis leaf spot).
symptoms: Angular brown to black leaf spots
Premature defoliation in severe cases
causes: Fungal spores spread by rain splash
Warm, humid conditions favoring infection
prevention: Manage canopy for good airflow
Remove and dispose of fallen infected leaves
management: Apply fungicide if disease pressure is high, per local extension guidance

name: Haunglongbing (Citrus Greening)
description: A serious bacterial disease of citrus caused by Candidatus Liberibacter species and spread by the Asian citrus psyllid. It is more commonly spelled "Huanglongbing" (HLB) in agricultural literature.
symptoms: Blotchy yellow mottling of leaves, often asymmetric across the midrib
Stunted tree growth
Small, lopsided, bitter-tasting fruit with aborted seeds
Twig dieback
causes: Bacterial infection transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid insect vector
Spread via infected grafting or propagation material
prevention: Control psyllid vector populations
Use certified disease-free planting material
Remove and destroy infected trees to limit spread
management: No cure is currently available; management focuses on vector control and orchard sanitation
Consult local agricultural authorities, as this disease is a regulated/quarantine concern in many regions

name: Bacterial Spot
description: A bacterial disease of peach caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, affecting leaves, twigs, and fruit.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked leaf spots that turn purple to brown
Leaf tissue may fall out, leaving a "shot-hole" appearance
Sunken lesions on fruit
causes: Bacterial infection favored by warm, wet, or windy weather
Spread by rain splash
prevention: Choose resistant varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
management: Apply copper-based bactericides where appropriate, per label and local extension guidance
Prune to improve air circulation

Avoid overhead irrigation

name: Early Blight
description: A fungal disease of potato caused by Alternaria solani.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric "target" rings, usually on older leaves first
Yellowing of tissue around spots
Leaves may die and drop prematurely
causes: Fungal spores overwintering in soil and plant debris
Warm, humid weather and plant stress favoring infection
prevention: Rotate crops away from potatoes and other solanaceous plants
Remove and dispose of infected plant debris
Space plants for good airflow
Maintain balanced fertilization
management: Apply fungicide per local extension guidance
Avoid overhead watering

name: Late Blight
description: A destructive disease of potato caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, historically associated with the Irish potato famine.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale-to-dark green lesions on leaves that rapidly turn brown or black
White, fungal-like growth on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Firm brown rot of tubers
causes: Spreads rapidly in cool, wet weather via windborne and waterborne spores
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes
Choose resistant varieties where available
Destroy volunteer potato plants
Avoid overhead irrigation
management: Apply fungicide promptly at the first sign of disease
Remove and destroy infected plants quickly to limit spread

Leaf yellowing and curling
Reduced plant vigor and yield in severe cases

Ensure good plant spacing and airflow
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization

symptoms: Small, irregular, deep purple spots on leaves
Spots may merge into larger scorched-looking blotches
Leaves may curl and dry out
causes: Favored by wet, humid conditions
Spread by rain splash
prevention: Remove old and infected leaves after harvest
Ensure good airflow and plant spacing
Avoid overhead irrigation
management: Apply fungicide where warranted per local extension guidance

Avoid working with wet plants

description: A fungal disease of tomato caused by Alternaria solani.
symptoms: Dark, concentric-ringed "target" spots, usually on older leaves first
Yellowing and defoliation
Dark, sunken lesions on stems and fruit
causes: Soil- and debris-borne fungal spores
Warm, humid weather and plant stress favoring infection
prevention: Rotate crops
Mulch to reduce soil splash onto leaves
Stake or cage plants for better airflow
Remove lower infected leaves
management: Apply fungicide per local extension guidance
Practice general garden sanitation

name: Late Blight
description: A destructive disease of tomato caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, capable of destroying a crop rapidly in favorable conditions.
symptoms: Large, water-soaked, green-to-black lesions on leaves
White fungal-like growth on leaf undersides in humid weather
Firm, dark rot on fruit
causes: Spreads quickly in cool, wet weather
prevention: Choose resistant varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation
Maintain good plant spacing
Destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants
management: Apply fungicide promptly at the first sign of disease
Rapidly remove and destroy infected plants to limit spread

name: Leaf Mold
description: A fungal disease of tomato caused by Passalora fulva (also known as Fulvia fulva), common in humid greenhouse and high-tunnel production.
symptoms: Pale yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to grayish-purple velvety mold on the leaf underside
causes: Favored by high humidity and poor air circulation
prevention: Improve ventilation, especially in greenhouses and tunnels
Reduce humidity around plants
Avoid overhead watering
Choose resistant varieties where available
management: Apply fungicide where warranted
Prune to improve airflow

name: Septoria Leaf Spot
description: A fungal disease of tomato caused by Septoria lycopersici, typically starting on lower, older leaves.
symptoms: Small, circular spots with dark margins and light gray-to-tan centers
Tiny black fruiting bodies visible within spot centers
Lower leaves affected first
causes: Favored by warm, humid weather
Spread by rain splash and overhead watering
prevention: Rotate crops
Mulch to reduce soil splash
Remove infected lower leaves
Avoid overhead irrigation
management: Apply fungicide per local extension guidance
Practice general garden sanitation

name: Two-Spotted Spider Mite
description: A pest infestation of tomato caused by the two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae). This is caused by an arachnid pest rather than a fungal, bacterial, or viral pathogen.
symptoms: Fine, light stippling or speckling on leaves
Leaf bronzing or yellowing
Fine webbing on leaf undersides in heavy infestations
causes: Favored by hot, dry, dusty conditions
Can worsen when broad-spectrum insecticides reduce natural predator populations
prevention: Monitor plants regularly for early signs of infestation
Maintain plant vigor and adequate watering
Reduce dust around plants
Conserve natural predators such as predatory mites
management: Use insecticidal soap, horticultural oil, or miticides where appropriate, per label guidance
A strong water spray can help dislodge mites in light infestations

name: Target Spot
description: A fungal disease of tomato caused by Corynespora cassiicola, producing lesions similar in appearance to early blight.
symptoms: Brown, concentric-ringed lesions on leaves
Lesions may also appear on stems and fruit
causes: Favored by warm, humid conditions
Spread by rain splash and wind
prevention: Rotate crops
Practice garden sanitation
Choose resistant varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation
management: Apply fungicide per local extension guidance

name: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
description: A viral disease of tomato transmitted by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of leaves
Stunted plant growth
Flower and fruit drop
Reduced yield
causes: Viral infection spread by whitefly feeding
Can also spread via infected transplants
prevention: Use virus-resistant varieties where available
Control whitefly populations
Use reflective mulches or row covers
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly
management: No cure once infected; management focuses on vector control and removing infected plants to reduce spread

name: Tomato Mosaic Virus
description: A highly stable viral disease of tomato that spreads mechanically through contact.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottling or mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaf distortion or fern-like narrowing
Stunted growth
Fruit discoloration
causes: Spread mechanically via hands, tools, contaminated seed, and plant-to-plant contact
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and transplants
Disinfect tools and hands between plants
Choose resistant varieties where available
Remove and destroy infected plants
management: No cure once infected; sanitation and prevention are the primary controls
